title: Product of Primes: Extending and Deepening Understanding nderstanding/
author: Dan Draper
summary: Dan Draper describes a set of tasks he wrote after moving schools and having to rethink his sequencing of product-of-primes content, part of a broader interest in how curriculum sequencing shapes what links teachers can emphasise. His first task uses variation -- holding the power of 17 constant throughout a column so students must reason about structural relationships rather than write out every expanded form -- before introducing reasoning with squares and cubes more explicitly in a second column. A second task pairs inequality reasoning about bases with the same power against reasoning about powers of ten, deliberately restricting the numbers used to primes, semi-primes, and square numbers so students focus on power relationships rather than getting bogged down finding products of primes. He then extends the sequence to finding roots via product of primes, noting that students often lack the flexibility to reason about commutativity as part of understanding why a method works, tending instead toward a rigid "find an answer" mindset. Draper closes by describing a final task that mirrors an earlier one but adds more explicit multiplication and division reasoning in its later questions, requiring students to find the product of primes before reasoning about the resulting powers of the roots involved.
points: Draper's first task keeps the power of 17 constant throughout a column specifically to force students to reason about structural relationships rather than default to writing out every expanded form.

He deliberately restricts a second task's numbers to primes, semi-primes, and square numbers so that power-relationship reasoning, not the mechanics of finding products of primes, stays the cognitive focus.

Draper identifies a specific misconception this sequencing targets: students often default to a rigid \"finding an answer\" mindset that overrides their willingness to reason about commutativity and structure.

The post is explicitly framed around curriculum sequencing after a school move, showing how the same underlying content (product of primes) gets restructured differently depending on what surrounding topics it connects to.
quotes: In moving schools, there’s often also a move in curriculum. Mostly, this affects the sequencing of content, and as such, the links you emphasise while teaching.
In this task, the first column uses variation to explore how changing the number alters it’s product of primes.
I’ve kept the power of 17 throughout the entire task to strong-arm pupils into considering the structural relationships with their powers rather than writing everything out in expanded forms.
When teaching this, I’ve found students lack the flexibility to think about commutativity when it forms part of the ‘why’ something works.
I think a lot of this comes down to the ‘finding an answer’ mindset that can override pupils’ willingness to play with structure.
